skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify top-level modules first (top-down), writing dependency specs on demand as verification drills down. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verification-order
skills.description: Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code, unjustified `uninterp spec fn` (use `detect_cheating`
  tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

1. **Removing `old(addrs)@.len() == 0` requires a spec change, not just an exec check**
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:287-325`, exec check at `332-337`
   - **Impact:** If `addrs` is non-empty, the function returns `Err`, but the current `Err` spec only allows `count == 0` or “no free range exists.” That will be false for valid `count` + available range.
   - **Fix:** Expand the `Err` postcondition to include the invalid-input case, e.g. `old(addrs)@.len() != 0 || count == 0 || forall|i| !range_free(...)`, plus state preservation.

2. **`count > num_pages` guard is likely the wrong fix**
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:339`, bitmap spec at `sparse-bitmap/lib.rs:1434-1458`
   - **Impact:** `bitmap.alloc_range(count)` already accepts any `count > 0` and returns `Err(OutOfMemory)` when no range exists. Adding an early `InvalidArgument` for `count > num_pages` changes observable behavior for no proof benefit.
   - **Fix:** Do **not** add the `count > num_pages` exec guard. Remove that precondition and prove the `Err` case from bitmap’s existing postcondition. At most, special-case `count == 0` if needed.

3. **Moving the wrappers to `mod.rs` does not really resolve the trusted-code issue**
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:73-99`
   - **Impact:** That just relocates the `external_body`; it doesn’t reduce trust or answer the reviewer’s concern.
   - **Fix:** Prefer:
     - `assume_specification[FrameAddress::from_raw_value]`, and
     - `assume_specification[<PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> as Address>::into_raw_value]`
     on the **concrete** type.  
     There is already precedent for concrete trait-method assumptions in `phys.rs:262`.

## Non-Blocking Issues

1. **`free()` guard is a real behavior change, not just proof scaffolding**
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:606-613`
   - **Impact:** Unlike `alloc_range`, this is fixing a real underflow hazard before subtraction. Good idea, but it changes exec behavior on invalid input.
   - **Fix:** Treat it as a bug fix explicitly. Validate non-Verus build/tests and, if you use exec-fidelity tooling, expect this to be a justified deviation.

2. **Your `addr < start => page_index < 0` proof needs care**
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:578-604`
   - **Impact:** The postcondition is probably right, but don’t rely on that arithmetic informally.
   - **Fix:** Prove `page_index < 0` (or directly `!input_valid`) with the actual Verus integer-division semantics, not just intuition.

## Suggestions

1. **For `alloc_range`, split the proof into three explicit error causes**
   - non-empty `addrs`
   - `count == 0`
   - bitmap failure for `count > 0`
   This will be cleaner than trying to force one proof path.

2. **Yes, replace deprecated `is_Ok()`**
   - Use `result matches Ok(_)` in any new assumption/spec.

## Direct answers

1. **Alloc-range runtime checks?**  
   - `count == 0`: acceptable if needed, though bitmap already handles it.  
   - `count > num_pages`: **no** — unnecessary and changes semantics.

2. **If trait-method `assume_specification` fails, is moving wrappers acceptable?**  
   - **No**. That’s just moving trusted code around.

3. **Missing verification implications?**  
   - The big one is the `addrs`-nonempty `Err` spec hole.  
   - Also, `free()` is a genuine exec behavior change and should be treated as such.

Overall: **good direction, but don’t add the oversize-count guard, and don’t forget to broaden the `alloc_range` error spec for non-empty `addrs`.**
